families.s: HSE duty-to-manage asbestos register, plan and information guidance
families.t: dutyholder scope, survey, register, risk assessment, management plan, monitoring, contractor information and emergency access
f: The duty to manage asbestos covers non-domestic premises and common parts of multi-occupancy domestic buildings.
Dutyholders should determine whether asbestos-containing materials may be present and arrange suitable surveys where needed.
An asbestos register should record locations, condition and areas not inspected.
The condition and likelihood of disturbance should be assessed.
A management plan should assign responsibility and state how identified materials will be managed and monitored.
The plan and register should be kept current as conditions and work change.
Employees, contractors and maintenance workers must receive relevant information before disturbing the building fabric.
Emergency services should be able to obtain information on known asbestos locations and condition.
families.g: Asbestos-management risk depends on building age and history, survey coverage, material type and condition, disturbance potential, register accuracy, communication, monitoring and work control.

families.s: HSE non-licensed and notifiable non-licensed asbestos-work guidance
families.t: risk classification, low intensity, control limit, material condition, notification, designated areas, medicals, health records and exposure control
f: Whether asbestos work is non-licensed depends on the task, material and exposure risk.
Non-licensed status does not remove the duty to prevent or adequately control exposure.
Work exempt from licensing must be sporadic and low intensity and remain below the legal control limit.
Short non-continuous work on non-friable material may qualify only when the specified conditions are met.
Some non-licensed work is notifiable because of the task, material type or condition.
NNLW requires notification to the enforcing authority and designation of the work area.
NNLW also requires medical examinations and maintenance of health or work records.
The employer must decide and document whether each job is licensed, NNLW or non-licensed before work begins.
families.g: Asbestos-work classification depends on material, friability and condition, task and duration, likely fibre release, control limit, worker exposure, notification and competence.

families.s: HSE licensed higher-risk asbestos-work and notification guidance
families.t: licensable criteria, contractor licence, sprayed coatings, insulation, AIB, notification, conditions, supervision and enforcing authority
f: Most higher-risk asbestos work must be carried out by a contractor licensed by HSE.
Licensable work includes work where exposure is not sporadic and low intensity or the control limit cannot clearly be met.
Work on sprayed asbestos, most insulation and most asbestos insulating board work normally requires a licensed contractor.
Employers must hold a licence before undertaking licensable work.
Ancillary work likely to disturb asbestos can also fall within licensable work.
Licensable work must normally be notified to the appropriate enforcing authority before it starts.
Licence conditions may restrict the work or require specific safety objectives.
Planning, supervision, air control, decontamination, medical surveillance and records must meet the applicable asbestos requirements.
families.g: Licensed-asbestos risk depends on material and friability, task, fibre release, enclosure and negative pressure, RPE, decontamination, supervision, licence scope and notification.

families.s: HSE manufactured-nanomaterial and high-aspect-ratio-material exposure-control guidance
families.t: COSHH assessment, uncertainty, CNTs, HARNs, substitution, containment, extraction, cleaning, RPE and disposal
f: Manufacture and manipulation of nanomaterials requires occupational exposure control under COSHH.
Guidance specifically addresses carbon nanotubes and other biopersistent high-aspect-ratio nanomaterials.
Emerging toxicology and uncertainty require a precautionary, proportionate control approach.
The assessment should identify material form, process, dust or aerosol generation and exposure routes.
Substitution, closed handling, containment and local extraction should be considered before PPE.
Cleaning methods should avoid redistributing dry nanomaterial contamination.
Suitable RPE and protective clothing may be required for residual exposure and maintenance.
Storage, spills, waste and decontamination should prevent uncontrolled release and secondary exposure.
families.g: Nanomaterial risk depends on particle type and shape, biopersistence, surface chemistry, agglomeration, process energy, airborne release, containment, cleaning, PPE and uncertainty.

families.s: HSE crane and lifting-operation planning, supervision and competence guidance
families.t: competent planning, method statements, supervision, crane stability, load control, exclusion, operators, slingers, signalling and examination
f: All lifting operations must be properly planned by a competent person, supervised and carried out safely.
Cranes and lifting accessories must have adequate strength and be inspected and examined as required.
Crane operators, slingers and people directing lifts must be trained and competent.
Crane collapse can create multiple-fatality risk both on and off site.
The plan should address crane selection, setup, stability, load, route, environment and foreseeable failure.
The crane supervisor should direct the operation in accordance with the method statement.
The supervisor needs authority to stop the operation when it is unsafe.
People not involved in the lift should be kept outside the danger zone of the crane and suspended load.
families.g: Lifting-operation risk depends on crane type and setup, ground bearing capacity, load mass and centre, radius, accessories, weather, route, competence, supervision and exclusion.
